Title: A hybrid framework for heart disease prediction using classical and quantum-inspired machine learning techniques
Author: Ankur Kumar; Sanjay Dhanka; Abhinav Sharma; Rohit Bansal; Mochammad Fahlevi; Fazla Rabby; Mohammed Aljuaid
Abstract: This research proposes a hybrid framework integrating classical and quantum-inspired machine learning techniques to enhance heart disease prediction. Using a combined UCI dataset and preprocessing/feature selection, the study trains and optimizes both classical and quantum-inspired SVM-based models evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation.
Method Used: Classical pipeline: CGA + CPSO + CSVM. Quantum-inspired pipeline (simulated): QGA + QPSO + QSVM using Qiskit Aer simulator.
Result: Quantum-inspired model: accuracy 97.83%, sensitivity 98.96%, specificity 96.59%, F1 97.94%, AUC 97%. Classical model: accuracy 94.02%. Runtime: 413.57s (quantum) vs 362.92s (classical).
Conclusion: Quantum-inspired hybrid outperformed classical hybrid across metrics while using fewer features; higher computational cost; demonstrated via classical simulation only.
Limitations: Quantum methods on classical simulators (not real QPU); increased runtime; no external validation on larger datasets; hardware noise/coherence constraints remain.
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, F1, AUC, LR+, LR-, DOR

Title: A primer for quantum computing and its applications to healthcare and biomedical research
Author: Thomas J.S. Durant; Elizabeth Knight; Brent Nelson; Sarah Dudgeon; Seung J. Lee; Dominic Walliman; Hobart P. Young; Lucila Ohno-Machado; Wade L. Schulz
Abstract: Introduces quantum computing technologies for biomedical research and highlights future applications in healthcare focusing on capabilities, benefits, limitations, and current state of hardware/software.
Method Used: Narrative literature review / primer — no original experimental model.
Result: Summarizes current quantum hardware is limited; QPUs should be viewed as accelerators complementary to CPUs/GPUs; practical quantum advantage for real-world biomedical tasks remains limited.
Conclusion: Quantum computing has promising potential for high-complexity biomedical problems but real-world advantages not yet broadly demonstrated; depends on hardware maturity and clearer benchmarking.
Limitations: Not a primary experimental study; conclusions depend on available literature; many cited applications constrained by current device scale/noise.

Title: A Quantum-Enhanced Precision Medicine Application to Support Data-Driven Clinical Decisions for the Personalized Treatment of Advanced Knee Osteoarthritis
Author: Nima Heidari; Stefano Olgiati; Davide Meloni; Mark Slevin; Ali Noorani; Federico Pirovano; Leonard Azamfirei
Abstract: QNN application to support precision data-driven clinical decisions to select personalized treatments for advanced knee osteoarthritis by classifying treatment responders vs non-responders.
Method Used: QNN (parameterized quantum circuit; Qiskit OpflowQNN); COBYLA optimizer; Aer simulator 1024 shots; train/test split 113/57.
Result: Test set (n=57): sensitivity 0.8235; specificity 0.2609; F1 0.7088; LR+ 1.1142; DOR 2.0. No information rate 0.59.
Conclusion: Preliminary validation suggests QML decision support for personalized treatment selection is promising but performance (especially specificity) is limited; requires larger datasets and clinical validation.
Limitations: Small validation dataset; low specificity/high false positives; outliers handling may affect generalizability; external validation required.
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Sensitivity, Specificity, F1, LR+, LR-, DOR

Title: A quantum-optimized approach for breast cancer detection using SqueezeNet-SVM
Author: Anas Bilal; Ali Alkhathlan; Faris A. Kateb; Alishba Tahir; Muhammad Shafiq; Haixia Long
Abstract: Proposes a hybrid approach Q-BGWO-SQSVM using quantum-inspired binary Grey Wolf Optimizer with SqueezeNet and SVM to enhance breast cancer classification accuracy.
Method Used: Mammogram preprocessing + Otsu thresholding segmentation + SqueezeNet feature extraction + SVM with Q-BGWO hyperparameter optimization; 5/10/15-fold CV on MIAS, INbreast, DDSM, CBIS-DDSM.
Result: Best on CBIS-DDSM with 15-fold CV: accuracy 99%, sensitivity 98%, specificity 100%.
Conclusion: Q-BGWO-SQSVM achieves near state-of-the-art mammography classification; reliable efficient approach for early breast cancer detection; further validation recommended.
Limitations: Reliance on benchmark datasets and cross-validation; clinical real-world deployment not validated; performance depends on preprocessing/ROI selection.
Classical Baseline Quality: Unclear — compared to prior literature only

Title: A systematic review of quantum machine learning for digital health
Author: Riddhi S. Gupta; Carolyn E. Wood; Teyl Engstrom; Jason D. Pole; Sally Shrapnel
Abstract: Systematic review assessing whether QML algorithms outperform existing classical methods for clinical decisioning or health service delivery. 4915 initial records; 169 eligible; 46 high-quality; 16 with realistic operating conditions.
Method Used: Systematic review (PRISMA; SPICE; PROSPERO); searched PubMed/Embase/IEEE/Scopus/arXiv 2015-2024; quality appraisal to 46 high-quality studies.
Result: No consistent empirical performance advantage of QML over classical methods in digital health; most studies rely on ideal simulations; only 16 used realistic operating conditions.
Conclusion: Current evidence base insufficient to claim empirical quantum utility in digital health; future work must establish scalability, uncertainty, noise robustness, and stronger benchmarking.
Limitations: Many studies excluded for low technical rigor; heterogeneous metrics impede meta-analysis; limited use of EHR/real-world datasets.

Title: A unifying nonlinear probabilistic epidemic model in space and time
Author: Roberto Beneduci; Eleonora Bilotta; Pietro Pantano
Abstract: Proposes a continuous space-time nonlinear probabilistic mother model for epidemic spread based on sub-probability densities; shows how multiple deterministic and stochastic epidemic models can be derived as special cases.
Method Used: Defines infected and susceptible sub-probability densities; derives coupled integro-differential equations; under locality/symmetry assumptions derives generalized Fisher-Kolmogorov-type drift-diffusion PDE; discretizes to obtain discrete stochastic processes.
Result: Key derivations: evolution equations for infected/susceptible densities; generalized Fisher-Kolmogorov with anomalous diffusion; classical Fisher-Kolmogorov arises from linearized probabilistic model.
Conclusion: Provides a unifying probabilistic framework connecting stochastic and deterministic epidemic models; forecasting applications depend on estimating kernel W from data.
Limitations: Assumes existence and differentiability of sub-probability densities; no births/deaths in base formulation; practical use depends on solving inverse problem to estimate kernel W from data.

Title: Advancing single-cell omics and cell-based therapeutics with quantum computing
Author: Aritra Bose; Kahn Rhrissorrakrai; Filippo Utro; Laxmi Parida; Quantum for Healthcare Life Sciences Consortium
Abstract: Roadmap article discussing how quantum computing could complement AI to address computational bottlenecks in spatiotemporal single-cell and spatial omics analysis.
Method Used: Narrative roadmap/review of quantum computing analogues for key single-cell/spatial analysis tasks; no new validated model.
Conclusion: Quantum computing may help overcome scaling, generalization, and sample-limited challenges in single-cell/spatial multi-omics; near-term utility depends on hardware maturity and careful benchmarking.
Limitations: Not yet clinically validated; many proposed approaches require fault-tolerant devices; major practical hurdles include data encoding overhead, noise/coherence limits, barren plateaus.

Title: An integrated strategy based on radiomics and quantum machine learning: diagnosis and clinical interpretation of pulmonary ground-glass nodules
Author: Xianzhi Huang; Fangyi Xu; Wenchao Zhu; Lin Yao; Jiahuan He; Junhao Su; Wending Zhao; Hongjie Hu
Abstract: Retrospective study developing integrated pipeline combining CT radiomics and QML (QSVC, Pegasos QSVC, QNN) with SHAP interpretability to classify pulmonary pGGNs as invasive vs non-invasive adenocarcinoma.
Method Used: CT pGGN segmentation + radiomics extraction (960 features) + Random Forest feature selection (9 features) + QML models (QSVC, Pegasos QSVC, QNN) on Qiskit noiseless simulator; SHAP interpretability.
Result: QNN: accuracy 89.23% (95% CI 81.54-95.38), sensitivity 96.55%, specificity 83.33%, AUC 0.937. QNN AUC significantly outperformed classical SVM AUC 0.833 (p=0.003).
Conclusion: Integrated radiomics + QML + SHAP improves pGGN invasiveness classification vs classical SVM; QNN performed best; supports use as non-invasive decision-support tool.
Limitations: Single-center retrospective design; relatively small sample; radiomics sensitive to scan parameters; SHAP visualization largely qualitative; scalability constrained by current quantum hardware.

Title: Applications of quantum computing in clinical care
Author: Stevan C. Fairburn; Lara Jehi; Brenton T. Bicknell; Beckley G. Wilkes; Bharat Panuganti
Abstract: Systematic review of quantum computing applications with first-order clinical relevance; summarizes evidence for impacts on diagnostics, treatment optimization, and real-time decision support.
Method Used: Systematic review across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science (Jan 2015-Jan 2024); screened 237 records; included 35 studies; thematic synthesis.
Result: QC promise across medical imaging and clinical decision-making (each 54.3% of included articles) and oncology (48.6%); many studies theoretical/simulation-based or use synthetic data.
Conclusion: Quantum computing shows potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency; clinical adoption limited by current technical, validation, and ethical constraints.
Limitations: Limited database scope; most included work theoretical/simulator-based/synthetic; heterogeneity limits generalizability; potential publication bias; lack of standardized benchmarks.

Title: Biology and medicine in the landscape of quantum advantages
Author: Benjamin A. Cordier; Nicolas P. D. Sawaya; Gian Giacomo Guerreschi; Shannon K. McWeeney
Abstract: Review proposing framework to define and classify quantum advantage and applying it across biology/medicine problems to assess where practical advantages may emerge.
Method Used: Narrative review + conceptual framework; surveys quantum algorithms and maps them to biomedical tasks; discusses practical constraints (NISQ vs FTQC).
Result: No new experimental results; quantum simulation (VQE) identified as most promising near-to-medium-term candidate; variational QML may offer potential benefits but requires further validation.
Conclusion: Quantum simulation for molecular systems is highlighted as the clearest near-term path to meaningful quantum advantage in biomedicine; variational/hybrid methods are key near-term strategy.
Limitations: No empirical data; theoretical framework only; timeline for operational advantage uncertain.

Title: Quantum-assisted federated intelligent diagnosis algorithm with variational training supported by 5G networks
Author: Arnaldo Rafael Camara Araujo; Ogobuchi Daniel Okey; Muhammad Saadi; Pablo Adasme; Renata Lopes Rosa; Demóstenes Zegarra Rodríguez
Abstract: Proposes β-QuAFIDA: a quantum-assisted federated learning framework for intelligent healthcare diagnosis via IoMT devices connected through 5G networks. Uses β-VQE optimization in a nested loop structure to preserve privacy and improve convergence.
Method Used: β-QuAFIDA: inner loop trains β-VQE to approximate expectation values; outer loop minimizes relative entropy to target. Implemented using PennyLane + PyTorch + QuEST simulator. Angle encoding. Tested on Fetal Health Dataset (2126 CTG records); 80/20 split.
Result: Central trained VQNN: test accuracy 83.90%. β-QuAFIDA (2 clients): 83.98%; (4 clients): 84.13%; (8 clients): 83.75%. Fidelity under noise: BF=0.9958, AD=0.9775, DN=0.9993. Personalized vs no personalized training: marginal gains.
Conclusion: β-QuAFIDA demonstrates robustness in noisy NISQ environments and suitable for privacy-preserving federated diagnosis; performance consistent across distributed configurations; promising for intelligent healthcare in 5G networks.
Limitations: Sensitivity to heuristic parameters R and α; tested on single dataset; no comparison to classical federated learning baselines; scalability to larger datasets not demonstrated; all quantum components simulated.
Classical Baseline Quality: No — no classical FL baseline reported

Title: IoT driven smart health monitoring for heart disease prediction using quantum kernel enhanced sardine diffusion and CNN
Author: Dibas Kumar Hembram; Satya Narayan Tripathy; CH Narsimha Reddy; Debabrata Dansana; Quadri Noorulhasan Naveed; Shafat khan; Mohammed Kareemullah; Addisu Frinjo Emma
Abstract: Proposes IoT-based Qua-KSar-DCK-ArNet for real-time heart disease prediction combining quantum clustering, Q2CNN, diffusion kernel attention, and Sardine Optimization Algorithm.
Method Used: Quantum Clustering with k-Means → Z-score Min-Max Normalization → Fast Point Transformer feature extraction → Q2CNN + DKAN (Qua-KSar-DCK-ArNet) with Sardine Optimization. UCI Heart Failure dataset (299 records). 70/15/15 split.
Result: Accuracy 99.97-99.98%; Precision 99.34-99.59%; Recall 98.47-99.56%; F1 96.34-99.46%; MSE 0.01; Specificity 99.27%; Training accuracy 99.9%; Execution time 0.1s.
Conclusion: Qua-KSar-DCK-ArNet achieves impressive 99% accuracy enabling real-time IoT-based diagnosis; future work to integrate additional physiological parameters and address scalability.
Limitations: Extremely small dataset (299 records); no confidence intervals; quantum components simulated not real hardware; no strong classical DNN baseline; 99%+ accuracy on 299-record dataset is unreliable indicator of generalizable performance.
Classical Baseline Quality: Weak — compared to non-DNN baselines only
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, MSE, Specificity
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Yes — claimed but dataset too small to establish

Title: Variational quantum classifier-based early identification and classification of chronic kidney disease using sparse autoencoder and LASSO shrinkage
Author: P. Parthasarathi; Haya Mesfer Alshahrani; K. Venkatachalam; Jaehyuk Cho
Abstract: QML-based technique for early diagnosis and prognosis of CKD using VQC with sparse autoencoder data augmentation and LASSO feature selection. Evaluated on UCI CKD dataset (400 patients, 25 attributes).
Method Used: Phase 1: Kalman filter + min-max normalization. Phase 2: Sparse autoencoder augmentation (KL divergence + L1). Phase 3: LASSO shrinkage (13 features selected). Phase 4: VQC (Qiskit RawFeatureVector + RealAmplitudes ansatz 3 layers + COBYLA + CrossEntropy loss).
Result: With LASSO: VQC accuracy 99.2%, precision 98.3%, recall 98.5%, F1 98.9%, AUC-ROC 99.1%. Without LASSO: VQC accuracy 98.2%. Outperforms SVM (92.8%), RF (90.7%), LR (93.9%), MLP (94.8%), QSVM (97.8%).
Conclusion: VQC with LASSO feature selection achieves 99.2% accuracy for CKD classification surpassing classical and quantum baselines; establishes groundwork for quantum-assisted medical AI systems.
Limitations: Quantum circuits susceptible to noise; scalability restricted by qubit/gate complexity; data encoding overhead; increased training time vs classical; tested only on UCI CKD dataset; no confidence intervals reported.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — SVM / RF / LR / MLP / QSVM compared
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Yes — outperforms all baselines on simulator
